methodology: ROS-responsive core crosslinked micelles were synthesized by combining enzymatic polymerization of a poly(ethylene glycol)-b-poly(thioketal) (mPEG-b-PTK) copolymer with thiol-ene click chemistry between the side chain double bond of mPEG-b-PTK and the thiol group of pentaerythritol tetrakis (3-mercaptopropionate). The stability, release rate, and cytotoxicity were characterized using DLS, TEM, NMR, AFM, SEM, in vitro release studies, and cell viability assays.
research_objective: To develop ROS-responsive polymer-based micelles for drug delivery in cancer treatment.

key_findings.finding: ROS-responsive core crosslinked micelles showed better stability and faster release of encapsulated doxorubicin (DOX) in acidic, hypoxic tumor microenvironment.
The ROS-responsive CCL micelles demonstrated good biocompatibility with low toxicity to HeLa cells and HUVEC cells.
ROS is a major endogenous stimulus in tumor microenvironment (TME) and overproduction of ROS can be used for drug targeting.
Polymerization of mPEG and M3 with a ratio of 1:7 yields copolymers with higher molecular weight (4700 Da) compared to the 1:10 ratio, which results in lower dispersity (1.37 vs 1.41).
Polymeric micelles synthesized from copolymers with a mPEG-b-PTK4 composition are stable and maintain high levels of ROS upon excessive dilution.
Characterization of polymeric micelles using multiple techniques including TEM, DLS, and 1H NMR.

Finally, flow cytometry and confocal laser scanning microscope (CLSM) showed that DOX-loaded micelles had excellent internalization efficiency in HeLa cells. In vitro drug release To further evaluate ROS-responsive behavior, the in vitro drug release performance of CCL and UCL DOX-loaded micelles was tested under physiological (pH 7.4) and oxidative conditions (pH 7.4 with 5 mM H2O2) to simulate the high ROS environment in tumor cells. As shown in Fig. 11, from 0 to 8 h, the release rate of both CCL and UCL DOX-loaded micelles in PBS containing 5 mM H2O2 was higher than that in PBS, respectively. Meanwhile, the release rate of UCL DOX-loaded micelles was higher than CCL DOX-loaded micelles in both environ- ments within the first 8 h, presumably because that the micelles were more stable after crosslinking, so the release rate was relatively slow at beginning. After 20 h, the release rate of CCL micelles in PBS containing 5 mM H2O2 exceeded that of UCL micelles, probably because the structure of CCL micelles was gradually destroyed by H2O2, resulting in faster release rate. Besides, the release rate of CCL DOX-loaded micelles approached 100% after 12 h in ABS (pH 6.0) with 5 mM H2O2 ucture of CCL micelles was gradually destroyed by H2O2, resulting in faster release rate. Besides, the release rate of CCL DOX-loaded micelles approached 100% after 12 h in ABS (pH 6.0) with 5 mM H2O2 (Fig. S8), which may because the amino group of DOX was protonated to improve the water solubility, so the release rate was quicker compared with under PBS (pH 7.4) conditions. 3.5. Cytotoxicity and cellular uptake The biocompatibility of empty micelles was evaluated using HeLa cells and HUVEC cells by MTT assay. It can be seen from Fig. 12 (A) and (B), when the concentration of CCL micelles increased to 800 mg/L, cell survival rates remained above 82% and 86%, respectively. This showed that the CCL micelles have good biocompatibility in both two cells. For UCL micelles, when concentration exceeds 200 mg/L, the cell survival rates dropped significantly and were about 40% and 30%, respectively, at the concentration of 800 mg/L. The high cytotoxicity of UCL micelles may be due to the presence of active acrylate structures in the carrier, indicating that the cytotoxicity of carrier can be reduced through crosslinking reactions. The toxicity of free doxorubicin, CCL/UCL DOX- loaded micelles, and doxorubicin hydrochloride in two cells was also measured, and the results were consistent. Different from DOX-loaded micelles that entered cells by endocytosis, free doxorubicin entered cells in the form of diffusion and was easily lost. At the same time, due to its poor solubility, so it had the least toxicity. And the cytotoxicity of CCL DOX-loaded micelles was less than UCL micelles, which may due to the delayed DOX release caused by the network structure formed in the hydrophobic core of CCL micelles.
